intro:
Mother’s Day is often the **mothers day restaurant busiest day** because people call for reservations, pickup orders, hours, and last-minute changes all at once. The phone can clog up fast, and that can cost you orders before a guest ever walks in.

The fix is simple: plan the phone like you plan the line in the kitchen. Use one clear script, forward calls the right way, and let ROAL handle the routine stuff like menu questions and pickup orders while your staff stays focused on service.

sections.h2: Why does Mother’s Day overwhelm the phone so fast?
sections.body:
Mother’s Day brings a mix of callers you do not always get on a normal Sunday. Some want a table. Some want pickup. Some need the address, parking, or hours. Some are calling from the car and want to know, "Can I add one more entree to my order?"

That is why the phone gets jammed. One busy line can block a reservation, a pickup order, and a customer who only needed the address. For many independent restaurants, the phone becomes the bottleneck before the dining room does.

A simple way to think about it:
- One call for a reservation
- One call for a pickup order
- One call for menu questions
- One call for "Are you open later today?"

If your team is already juggling the front counter, the kitchen, and curbside handoff, the phone can fall behind. That is the exact kind of rush ROAL is built for as an AI phone host for restaurants. It answers the phone, takes pickup and delivery orders from your live menu, and sends a clean ticket to the kitchen screen.

sections.h2: What should I set up before Mother’s Day starts?
sections.body:
Do the prep work before the rush starts. The goal is to make the phone easy for callers and easy for your team.

Use this checklist:
1. Check your hours for the holiday.
2. Confirm your menu items, prices, and sold-out items.
3. Decide who handles reservations, catering, and allergy-sensitive calls.
4. Make sure your call forwarding still works.
5. Put one person on phone follow-up if questions need a human answer.

Here is a simple script line staff can use: "Thanks for calling. We’re busy right now, but I can help with pickup, menu questions, or reservations."

sections.h2: How should I forward calls on a holiday rush?
sections.body:
Forwarding is one of the easiest ways to protect your main line on a holiday. The exact code depends on your carrier and plan, so confirm it and test it with a real call before Mother’s Day.

Common examples include:
- Many landlines and some carriers: *72 to forward all calls, *73 to turn it off
- AT&T and T-Mobile GSM mobile service: **21*number# for all calls, ##21# to turn it off
- Unanswered calls: **61*number#
- Busy calls: **67*number#
- Verizon Wireless: *72 / *73, and *71 for busy/no-answer forwarding
- Business VoIP systems: often set forwarding in the web portal

A practical setup for Mother’s Day:
- Forward all calls to your phone host during the lunch and dinner rush
- Forward only unanswered or busy calls if you still want the front desk to ring first
- Turn forwarding off after service ends

ROAL gives each location its own phone line automatically after you claim the host, and you can forward your existing number to it. You keep your number, and you can turn forwarding off any time.

sections.h2: What phone script keeps the line moving without sounding rude?
sections.body:
A good holiday script should be short, calm, and direct. The caller should know what the restaurant can handle right now.

Try this structure:
1. Greet the caller.
2. Say what you can help with.
3. Ask for the next piece of information.
4. Confirm the order or reservation.

Example script:
"Thanks for calling. I can help with pickup orders and menu questions right now. What can I get started for you?"

If the caller wants a normal pickup order, keep it moving:
- Name
- Phone number
- Items, sizes, modifiers, and notes
- Ready time
- Repeat the order back

If they ask for something special, hand it to staff with a summary. ROAL does this for catering, complaints, allergy-sensitive questions, and manager requests. It also speaks the caller’s language and can take reservations. That helps the phone stay useful even when the dining room is packed.

sections.h2: How do I judge whether the phone rush is worth the cost?
sections.body:
Use your own numbers. Do not guess. A simple example can help you see the size of the opportunity.

Say your average pickup order is $28. If you miss 10 orders on a holiday weekend, that is $280 in order value. If you miss 25 orders, that is $700. Plug in your own average order and your own missed-call count.

Now compare that with common phone costs:
| Option | How it is often priced |
| --- | --- |
| Delivery apps | Roughly 15-30% commission per order |
| Human answering services | Usually per minute or per call |
| Many AI phone tools | Often a monthly fee per location |
| ROAL | $0.90 per completed phone order, with no monthly fee |

That does not mean one option is always best. It means the cost should match the work. If Mother’s Day brings a wave of pickup and delivery calls, pay-per-order pricing can be easier to map to actual demand. sections.h2: What should staff do with tricky calls and special requests?
sections.body:
Not every call should be handled like a standard order. Some calls need a person, especially when the caller is upset or needs something outside the menu.

Set a simple handoff rule:
- Allergy-sensitive questions go to staff
- Catering requests go to staff
- Complaint calls go to staff
- Manager requests go to staff
- Anything the phone host cannot answer goes to the inbox

That inbox matters. The owner answers the question once, and ROAL knows it from then on. That keeps the same question from landing on your team again and again.

You can also save time with a short handoff note. Example: "Caller wants a gluten-free option, asked about parking, and may need a larger order for Sunday evening." That way your team does not have to listen to the whole call again.

sections.h2: What should I do after Mother’s Day ends?
sections.body:
After the rush, spend 15 minutes tightening the next holiday setup. The goal is to make the next busy day easier than the last one.

Use this post-holiday checklist:
1. Review call history and transcripts.
2. Check which questions came up again and again.
3. Update hours, menu items, or FAQs.
4. Remove sold-out items from the menu.
5. Adjust forwarding so it matches your normal schedule again.

If you use ROAL, the dashboard shows live tickets, call history with transcripts and recordings, the menu editor, hours, FAQs, upsell suggestions, and multi-location menus. That makes it easier to see what happened on the rush and fix the weak spots.

takeaways: Mother’s Day can flood your phone with reservations, pickup orders, and menu questions.
Forwarding should be tested before the rush, not during it.
A short script keeps calls moving and reduces confusion.
ROAL can take routine orders and send special calls to staff with a summary.
Use your own order value and missed-call count to judge the real cost.

faq.q: Why is Mother’s Day such a busy day for restaurant phones?
faq.a: People call for reservations, pickup orders, hours, parking, and last-minute changes all at the same time. That creates a phone bottleneck even when the dining room is ready. The fix is to simplify the phone flow before service starts.

faq.q: Should I forward all calls or only busy and unanswered calls on Mother’s Day?
faq.a: It depends on how busy your front desk is. Forwarding all calls works when you want the phone host to handle everything, while busy or unanswered forwarding is better when staff still need to answer some calls first. Always confirm the code with your carrier or phone system and test it with a real call.
